transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jia Chen (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (Aurora CTO), Ben Park (Lead ML Eng), Amira Hassan (Infra)

Summary:
Brief deep dive on KV cache evictions, paging behavior under long-context workloads, and prefix reuse strategies. Aurora seeing increased perplexity/latency spikes when context exceeds ~65k tokens; suspected KV thrash and eviction churn. Discussed short-term mitigations and long-term architecture options (disk-backed paging, pinning hot prefixes, eviction-policy tuning).

Topics: KV cache size and eviction policy, paging to CPU/NVMe, long-context inference patterns, prefix reuse/pinning, telemetry/logging, batching/quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem implications for disk paging.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to keep this technical, i think jia's gonna drive the deep dive. lena, ben, amira you good with the agenda?
[00:06] Lena: yep, sounds good. i can share quick context: we've got a multi-user assistant that keeps conversation history and documents in the prompt, and once sessions hit around 60-70k tokens we see token latency jump and sometimes model outputs degrade.
[00:18] Ben: to add, the pattern is not constant — some sessions run fine, others blow up. we've instrumented latency spikes to correlate with an uptick in KV cache evictions and paging events in the runtime logs.
[00:27] Jia: okay that's consistent with eviction churn. quick question: are you running prefix reuse/pinning for system prompts or doc embeddings?
[00:33] Ben: we tried pinning the system prompt but only for short sessions. for longer doc prefixes, we haven't pinned because we thought it'd be memory-heavy.
[00:40] Jia: got it. two main failure modes — pure eviction due to insufficient KV memory, and thrashing where hot prefixes get evicted then reloaded due to interleaved user sessions. both cause latency regressions because page-ins are expensive.
[00:50] Amira: on infra side we're on dedicated GPUs with a 1.8 TB GPU mem pool per node, but KV allocation is per-model instance and we use default LRU eviction.
[00:58] Samir: quick note: LRU is simple but can punish workloads with periodic reuse patterns. for example, prefix reuse across sessions can beat LRU if the reuse period is longer than cache window.
[01:07] Jia: exactly. we often recommend either increasing KV capacity or switching to an ARC-like policy when workloads have non-uniform reuse. ARC is more adaptive between recency and frequency.
[01:16] Ben: is ARC supported in the runtime today?
[01:19] Jia: we have an experimental ARC variant in 1.18 runtime builds; stable LRU remains default. ARC helps for mixed workloads but adds CPU overhead for bookkeeping. tradeoff is CPU vs reduced page I/O.
[01:28] Lena: what about paging — you mentioned disk-backed paging earlier?
[01:31] Jia: yes. two approaches: 1) CPU RAM-backed KV paging (fast but limited by host RAM), 2) NVMe-backed paging — cheaper capacity but higher latency. NVMe can be viable if you prefetch and use async IO to hide latency, but worst-case tail delays still increase.
[01:42] Amira: we currently don't allow runtime NVMe on our VPC setup for compliance — disallowed by our infra policy. is there a way to do it without leaving control plane?
[01:50] Samir: for Private deployments we can package NVMe as an on-prem option with customer-managed encryption and access controls; that's been done for other enterprise customers. for cloud VPCs, there are marketplace AMI options. we'll share a reference architecture.
[02:01] Ben: curious about long-context and batch interactions. we batch requests to improve throughput, but does batching make eviction worse?
[02:07] Jia: batching increases concurrent KV working set because requests in a batch may touch different prefixes, increasing memory pressure. balancing batch size vs latency SLO is key; for long-contexts you often need smaller batch sizes or request-level routing to dedicated instances with larger KV allocations.
[02:21] Ben: so possible mitigations: reduce batch size for sessions with long contexts, or route them to nodes with bigger KV. can we detect and auto-route?
[02:27] Jia: yes — smart routing by policy is in the platform: route by predicted context length or customer tag to nodes with larger KV config. we discussed config earlier: pin certain prefixes (like doc embeddings) so they don't evict, and raise kv_max_entries for models serving long-context.
[02:40] Lena: pinning sounds great, but how do we keep it from consuming too much memory for multi-tenant clusters?
[02:45] Jia: two strategies: 1) pin on a per-customer dedicated node (Dedicated mode) so isolation prevents others from suffering, or 2) use soft-pinning with eviction priority — pinned prefixes get high priority but still evict under absolute memory pressure, and we expose metrics to monitor hit-rate impact.
[02:58] Amira: Are there telemetry signals we should capture to tune this? we already export Prometheus metrics but might be missing finer-grained traces.
[03:04] Jia: key metrics: kv_hits, kv_misses, kv_evictions, kv_page_in_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), per-prefix reference count, and per-session working set size. collecting sample KV traces on evictions shows which prefixes thrash. we can provide a tracing checklist.
[03:17] Samir: action item, samir will share docs and jia will provide the trace checklist.
[03:22] Ben: another question: we use 4-bit quantized models for cost. does quantization affect KV behavior?
[03:27] Jia: model quantization mostly affects compute memory and throughput; it doesn't change KV structure, but quantized models sometimes increase token generation time which can change request concurrency patterns — indirectly affecting KV working set. also some kernel choices change how KV is stored or compressed.
[03:41] Lena: we saw periods where inference CPU spiked and that correlated with paging. could that be due to decompression of cached KV when moving from NVMe->GPU?
[03:49] Jia: possibly. if KV entries are compressed or frozen on NVMe, page-in requires decompression CPU cycles. that's why async prefetch and offloading decompression to spare CPU cores can help. also avoid synchronous page-ins on the critical path.
[04:03] Ben: we touched evictions involving prefix reuse — our assistant uses a handful of long doc prefixes across many sessions but interleaves user prompts. sometimes those prefixes get evicted and then re-requested causing re-computation. best fix besides pinning?
[04:15] Jia: consider sharding prefixes across nodes by affinity — collocate hot prefixes with their session traffic. that reduces cross-node cache misses. also prefix-level TTLs: set a reuse TTL window based on observed reuse frequency so the runtime keeps entries for the expected reuse period.
[04:31] Amira: what about fallback behavior? when a cache miss occurs, what's the expected latency delta?
[04:37] Jia: depends. in-memory page-in from host RAM is tens of ms; NVMe page-in can be 50-200ms depending on prefetch and IO patterns; full recompute (if we need to re-encode prefix) can be several hundred ms to seconds. those numbers line up with what you reported, right ben?
[04:52] Ben: yes, many of our spikes are 100-400ms per token chunk and correlate with NVMe page-ins.
[04:58] Samir: a concrete near-term plan: 1) increase kv_max_entries for affected model pool by 20% to reduce eviction frequency, 2) enable soft-pinning for system and top N doc prefixes, 3) run a targeted benchmark with pinned prefixes and smaller batch sizes, 4) instrument and collect traces.
[05:12] Lena: what's the risk to throughput/cost if we increase kv memory?
[05:16] Jia: bigger KV reduces page I/O but increases memory footprint per instance, which can lower consolidation (fewer instances per GPU) and raise cost. cost vs latency tradeoff as usual. Redwood can run cost simulations — we have a tool that estimates unit token cost given kv_size, batch_size, and model.
[05:30] Ben: for our dedicated nodes can we change eviction policy per-pool?
[05:33] Jia: yes, eviction policy is configurable per-model-pool. you can roll out ARC on a canary pool first to measure CPU overhead and hit-rate improvement.
[05:41] Amira: log formats — when we look at runtime logs for page-in events there are object IDs that look opaque. can you provide guidance on mapping object IDs to prefixes?
[05:49] Jia: we'll share a mapping utility; runtime emits prefix hash and session id, and we can translate hashes to human-readable prefix keys if you enable debug mapping (we'll redact PII). that's part of the trace checklist.
[06:02] Ben: any thoughts on multi-tenant vs dedicated model instances — we lean toward multi-tenant to save cost but these long-context sessions are a pain.
[06:11] Jia: for multi-tenant, you need stronger QoS: per-tenant soft limits, priority pinning, and route-based isolation. Dedicated mode obviously simplifies but costs more. Sometimes hybrid works: put heavy long-context customers into dedicated pools and leave the rest multi-tenant.
[06:25] Lena: what's the roadmap for more advanced paging? like hierarchical caches?
[06:29] Jia: we're experimenting with a 3-tier approach: on-GPU KV (fastest), host-RAM cache (medium), NVMe (largest). smart prefetch uses access patterns to promote items. also looking at approximate membership filters to avoid unnecessary page-ins. will be part of upcoming runtime 1.20 experimental features.
[06:45] Ben: can we simulate our workload on Redwood test cluster?
[06:48] Samir: yes, we'll provision a dedicated canary cluster and run your session traces, with options to toggle page store (RAM vs NVMe), eviction policy, and batch sizes. that's part of the benchmark plan.
[06:58] Amira: security question: if we enable NVMe paging, does it change our encryption/compliance posture?
[07:04] Samir: NVMe on Private deployments can be encrypted at rest using your KMS/HSM; for hosted we use encrypted volumes and strict IAM. we'll provide the security docs and a compliance checklist.
[07:15] Jia: small gotcha — when using disk paging, make sure to set io_scheduler and ensure low-latency NVMe with enough parallelism; some cloud attachments can have unpredictable tail latencies.
[07:25] Ben: for the benchmark, what metrics should we capture aside from kv_* ?
[07:29] Jia: capture end-to-end token latency p50/p95/p99, kv_page_in_latency p50/p95/p99, cpu utilization (per-core), gpu utilization, batch sizes, memory pressure, and per-prefix hit rate. also capture per-session working set size.
[07:44] Samir: also we'll gather cost estimates for each config so you can make an economics tradeoff.
[07:50] Lena: Anything else on quantization or batching?
[07:53] Jia: watch for batch-induced working set expansion as mentioned. for quantization, test both compute latency and concurrency changes — 4-bit may change how many concurrent requests you can serve, which indirectly relates to KV pressure.
[08:05] Ben: one last operational question: during model rollouts we sometimes see cache invalidation across instances; is there a recommended pattern?
[08:12] Jia: best practice: warm caches pre-rollout by replaying typical prefixes to the new model instances, or use phased canary rollout with overlap so old instances serve until new ones warm. avoid full simultaneous cutover. also persist hot-prefix mapping so you can rehydrate quickly.
[08:27] Amira: good tips.
[08:29] Samir: ok wrap up — recap of next steps and who owns what.
[08:33] Lena: thanks everyone.

Notes/References:
- Shared doc: https://redwood.internal/kv-cache-tuning (Samir to share)
- Trace checklist & mapping utility: Jia to send
- Benchmark plan: Ben/Aurora to run and share logs

End of transcript.
